The diaries chronicle Gerald's increasingly unhinged journey through Excretion Court, where attorneys cite landmark precedents like *The State v. One Rogue Bladder*, jurors solemnly evaluate stool sample evidence chains, and Gerald ping-pongs between genuine hope (an obscure loophole in the Urination Codex of 1987) and bowel-loosening terror (mobs outside the courthouse demanding his "Final Flush," this world's capital punishment). What makes the tapes so infamous in this parallel history is what Gerald gradually, profanely pieces together: Maureen Trask herself operates a clandestine network of unmonitored luxury toilets for the political elite, and she weaponized the accusation against Gerald specifically because he'd unknowingly audited one of her secret facilities—meaning the only person who can expose the most powerful woman in the country is a man the entire civilization now considers a shit-smeared monster.

# Seven Structural Beats for *The Surviving Audio Diaries of Gerald Pfeiffer, Certified Flush Auditor*

---

## Beat 1: The Tapes Surface — The Archival Frame and the Missing Recordings

**What Must Happen:** An editorial or curatorial voice introduces the audio diaries — perhaps a historian, an archivist at the Bureau of Biological Compliance's post-scandal records division, or a journalist who obtained the tapes through a freedom-of-information equivalent. The voice establishes that these are the "sole surviving" recordings of Gerald Pfeiffer, that several tapes are missing or damaged (one was reportedly confiscated, another is water-damaged, a third appears to have been recorded over with what sounds like Bureau-mandated bowel-movement affirmations). Gerald's voice enters mid-thought, possibly mid-complaint, on a tape that is clearly not the first.

**Structural Function — The False Document, Scatological Variant:** Like Borges's missing two pages, the incomplete archive must do triple duty. First, it simulates authenticity: real bureaucratic records are always incomplete, redacted, misfiled. Second, it creates urgency: we have arrived after something has already gone wrong, and Gerald is already afraid. Third — and this is the thematic key — it establishes that *this society's power operates through control of documentation*. A civilization that tracks every bowel movement is a civilization of total record-keeping. The missing tapes are therefore not just a narrative convenience but an act of violence by the system the story will indict. Someone made those tapes disappear. The gaps in Gerald's record mirror the gaps in the Bureau's surveillance — the unmonitored luxury toilets that are the story's secret. **The archive is incomplete for the same reason the conspiracy exists: the powerful decide what gets recorded.**

**What Must Make It Land:** Gerald's voice, from the first moment, must be simultaneously pathetic and precise. He is a mid-level auditor — a man whose entire professional identity is procedural rigor — and that voice should come through even as he is clearly unraveling. The comedy lives in the gap between bureaucratic diction and existential terror. His first recorded words should betray both: the language of compliance reports applied to the experience of having his life destroyed. The curatorial frame should be dry, institutional, and subtly unreliable — there should be a faint suggestion that the entity presenting these tapes has its own reasons for doing so.

---

## Beat 2: The Accusation — Gerald Learns He Is the Rogue Voider

**What Must Happen:** Gerald recounts (or we hear in near-real-time) the moment the accusation becomes public. Director Maureen Trask — whose voice he may describe with the particular reverence this society apparently affords her — has named him. The charge: off-grid defecation, biological terrorism, Rogue Voiding. Gerald describes what this means in practical terms: his Compliance Profile is flagged, his FlushPass is revoked, his neighbors have already placed biohazard tape across his driveway. He explains, for the audience of himself (these are private diaries), what a Rogue Voider *is* in this civilization — and his explanation must make clear that this is not a misdemeanor but a charge equivalent to releasing a plague. He also explains, with escalating indignation, that he has never once voided off-grid, that his personal output logs are *immaculate*, that he once reported himself for a 0.3-second flush-delay discrepancy.

**Structural Function — The Decision Under Pursuit, Inverted:** Where Borges's Yu Tsun makes a cold tactical calculation (find Albert, kill him, transmit the name), Gerald must be shown as a man with *no plan and no viable motivation*. This is essential. His spy-thriller equivalent is not a daring scheme but a bureaucratic reflex: he will fight this through proper channels, through the Excretion Court system, because *the system is all he has ever believed in*. His faith in procedure is his defining trait and his fatal flaw. The comedy and the tragedy must be welded here: Gerald is the truest believer in the institution that is destroying him. His motivation is not spite (like Yu Tsun's) but something more pitiable — *compliance as identity*. He wants to be proven clean not because he values freedom but because he values his record.

**What Must Make It Land:** Maureen Trask must be established here not as a distant villain but as a figure Gerald *admires*. He should reference her with the involuntary reverence of a functionary for his highest superior — perhaps quoting one of her public slogans, perhaps recalling a Bureau-wide address that moved him. The accusation must feel like a parent's betrayal, not an enemy's attack. This emotional asymmetry is what will power the entire story: Gerald is being destroyed by someone he would have died to serve. The mobs demanding his "Final Flush" should be rendered through Gerald's audio descriptions — chants heard from inside his apartment, sounds bleeding through windows — so that the threat is acoustic, claustrophobic, mediated through the same recording technology that structures the whole narrative.

---

## Beat 3: Excretion Court — The Procedural Labyrinth

**What Must Happen:** Gerald's tapes now chronicle his entry into the legal system. He describes, in appalled and granular detail, the proceedings of Excretion Court: the attorneys (his own is a "Certified Bowel Barrister" who inspires no confidence), the precedents cited with grave solemnity (*The State v. One Rogue Bladder*, *In Re: Fourteen Unregistered Movements*, the landmark *Duodenal Rights Act*), the jurors who are specially screened for "output neutrality," the evidence chain for stool samples that is treated with the forensic gravity of DNA at a murder trial. Gerald ping-pongs between hope and terror. He discovers what he believes is a genuine loophole — an obscure clause in the Urination Codex of 1987 that may create an evidentiary exception — and records himself reading it aloud, voice trembling with relief that is audibly premature.

**Structural Function — The Lane of Forking Paths / World-Building as Disguised Thesis:** This beat is where the world must be built in full, and the world-building must be simultaneously hilarious and structurally load-bearing. Every absurd legal detail — every solemnly cited precedent, every procedural formality around fecal evidence — must function the way the children's instruction "turn left at every fork" works in Borges: *it must sound like local color while actually encoding the story's thesis*. The thesis is: **a surveillance state that controls the body's most basic functions will inevitably produce a legal system of baroque, self-serious complexity that exists not to find truth but to perform legitimacy for a system that is, at its core, about power over the most intimate aspects of human life.** The courtroom is the labyrinth. Gerald's careful navigation of it (his hope in the Urination Codex loophole) is structurally equivalent to Yu Tsun following the lane — it *feels* like agency within a system that has already determined his destination.

**What Must Make It Land:** The comedy must be played with absolute tonal commitment. Gerald must never wink. He must describe stool-sample chain-of-custody protocols with the same seriousness a real defendant would describe DNA evidence, because *to him this is real*. The humor for the reader/listener emerges from the gap between Gerald's earnest procedural faith and the patent absurdity of what he's describing — but this gap must never become contempt. The reader must, against all reason, start to feel the procedural hope Gerald feels when he finds the Urination Codex loophole. That hope must be *real enough to be crushed later*. Buried in this beat, disguised as another piece of courtroom minutiae or an offhand complaint, Gerald should mention — almost in passing — the audit that started everything. He should reference an inspection report he filed on a facility whose address or designation struck him as odd. This is the premature disclosure: **the answer to the story's mystery is given here, openly, and the reader walks right past it because it is camouflaged as bureaucratic grumbling.**

---

## Beat 4: The Anomalous Audit — Gerald Begins to See the Pattern

**What Must Happen:** Under the pressure of preparing his defense, Gerald revisits his old audit files — perhaps he has physical copies, perhaps he's reconstructing from memory, perhaps he convinces his hapless Bowel Barrister to subpoena his own work records. He returns, on tape, to the audit that preceded his accusation: an inspection of a facility that was listed in Bureau records but whose specifications didn't match standard infrastructure. The toilet fixtures were wrong — too luxurious, unmetered, lacking the federally mandated Deposit Verification Sensors. Gerald describes realizing, perhaps slowly over the course of one or two diary entries, that the facility was not just non-compliant but *deliberately unmonitored*. Someone built a place where important people could void without record. And then, with a chill audible in his voice, he connects the date of his audit report's filing to the date Trask's office initiated the Rogue Voider accusation against him.

**Structural Function — The Recognition / Uncanny Convergence:** This beat mirrors Albert's garden: the moment where the spy plot and the deeper plot visibly converge, where the protagonist discovers that the two things he thought were separate (his prosecution and his professional work) are the same structure. The uncanny element here is not cultural chiasmus (as in Borges) but *institutional* chiasmus: the system Gerald devoted his career to serving has a shadow version of itself, and the shadow version is the real one. The compliant world (tracked toilets, Flush Auditors, Excretion Court) exists to conceal and protect the non-compliant world (Trask's luxury network). Gerald's meticulous auditor's eye — the very faculty that makes him a perfect bureaucrat — is what made him dangerous, and what makes him, in this moment, the only person capable of recognizing the truth. **He is the descendant entering the ancestor's labyrinth: the man whose professional faith is the tool that disassembles the institution he worships.**

**What Must Make It Land:** The revelation must arrive not as a single thunderclap but as a pattern Gerald assembles across tape entries, the way a real person thinking alone would: with false starts, reversals, moments of self-doubt ("Am I losing it? Is this what happens to Rogue Voiders — they start seeing conspiracies in the plumbing?"), and then a sudden, profane, undeniable recognition. Gerald's diary voice should shift here. The bureaucratic diction that has been his armor should crack, and something rawer should emerge — not eloquence, but the stumbling articulacy of a man whose entire worldview is restructuring in real time. The emotional equivalent of Albert's garden is this: Gerald finds something *beautiful* in the conspiracy's design, despite himself. The network is *elegant*. It is, in its way, a masterpiece of the very auditing principles he reveres, turned inside out. He should be horrified and, for one terrible moment, impressed.

---

## Beat 5: The Full Architecture of the Conspiracy — Gerald's Ontological Revelation

**What Must Happen:** Gerald, now in full investigative frenzy, pieces together the complete scope of Trask's operation. He describes it into his recorder with the manic precision of a man who knows he may not get to describe it again. Trask's clandestine network is not a few rogue toilets — it is a parallel infrastructure, a shadow Bureau, serving the political elite who publicly champion the most draconian output-compliance laws while privately voiding in unmonitored luxury. The system requires Rogue Voider scapegoats: public enemies whose prosecutions justify increased surveillance budgets, which fund both the visible Bureau *and* its invisible twin. Gerald realizes he is not an accident of the system but a *product* of it. The Rogue Voider accusation is not a malfunction — it is the machine working as designed. Every Rogue Voider trial in history may have been manufactured.

**Structural Function — The Embedded Lecture as Conceptual Climax:** As in Borges, the story's true climax is not an action but a *comprehension*. Gerald's discovery retroactively reorganizes everything the reader has experienced: the courtroom's baroque solemnity, the public's genuine terror of Rogue Voiders, Trask's beloved public persona, the missing tapes from the archive. Every detail of the world-building, which seemed like comic invention, is revealed as a component of a functioning machine of oppression. This is the story's ontological anagnorisis: Gerald (and the reader) recognize that the *genre* they thought they were in — absurdist bureaucratic comedy — is actually dystopian horror, and always was. The laughter was real, but what was funny was a atrocity. The Urination Codex loophole Gerald pinned his hopes on is revealed here, implicitly or explicitly, as part of the design: a hope-valve built into the legal system to keep defendants compliant through the trial process.

**What Must Make It Land:** Gerald must articulate the conspiracy clearly enough that the reader grasps the full mechanism, but he must do so in his voice — profane, digressional, terrified, occasionally still funny in spite of himself. The revelation should carry a specific emotional charge beyond horror: *loneliness*. Gerald now understands something that no one will believe, spoken into a recorder that may never be heard, by a man the entire civilization considers subhuman. The parallel to Albert explaining the garden of forking paths is precise: here too, the only person who fully understands the system is in a room with the only person capable of receiving the knowledge, except Gerald's room contains only himself. The recorder is his Stephen Albert — an audience that listens with perfect attention and cannot help him at all.

---

## Beat 6: The Final Tape — Gerald's Act and Its Cost

**What Must Happen:** Gerald takes an action. The specifics must feel both inevitable and shocking. Perhaps he smuggles his evidence into the court record through the one mechanism the Bureau cannot suppress (his own stool sample submission — hiding documentation literally *inside* the evidence chain, a move of such grotesque procedural genius that it could only occur to a true Flush Auditor). Perhaps he broadcasts his tapes through a method the curatorial frame has already hinted at. Perhaps he confronts Trask directly and records it. Whatever the act, it must be compressed — rendered in as few sentences as the story's tone allows — after the expansive revelation of Beat 5. And it must cost him something irreversible. The Final Flush may be carried out. Madden arrives; the gun fires. Gerald may not survive his own story.

**Structural Function — Compression and Structural Irony:** Like Yu Tsun's murder of Albert, Gerald's climactic act must be the point where the satirical plot and the human plot fuse into a single gesture. The act that exposes Trask (the satirical/political victory) must simultaneously destroy something Gerald values — perhaps his last shred of procedural faith, perhaps his life, perhaps his dignity in a way he cannot recover. The structural irony should mirror Borges: **Gerald must use the very system that persecuted him as the vehicle for his revelation, meaning his act of resistance is also an act of compliance.** He fights the Bureau *through Bureau channels*. He defeats the labyrinth by walking deeper into it. He is, in the end, the perfect auditor — and that perfection is both his weapon and his cage. narrative_story:
# The Surviving Audio Diaries of Gerald Pfeiffer, Certified Flush Auditor

---

## EDITOR'S NOTE

*The following transcripts are drawn from the fourteen surviving analog microcassettes of Gerald R. Pfeiffer (Bureau ID: FA-4409-GL), recovered during the 2037 decommissioning of the Bureau of Biological Compliance's Northeast Regional Processing Center. Of an estimated thirty to thirty-five original recordings, twenty-one are unaccounted for. Tapes 1 through 4 have never been located. Tape 9 was confiscated by the Bureau's Internal Suppression Office during the Pfeiffer proceedings and is presumed destroyed per standard protocol. Tape 11 is water-damaged beyond salvage. Tape 17 was recorded over — apparently by a subsequent occupant of the storage unit — with what audio analysts have identified as sixty-eight minutes of the Bureau-mandated Bowel Affirmation Cycle, a guided recitation exercise once distributed to Compliance Tier employees. ("I release with gratitude. I release with purpose. My output is my gift to the monitored community.") We have been unable to determine whether the overwriting was accidental or policy.*

*The remaining tapes were authenticated in 2039 by three independent audio forensics laboratories, cross-referenced against Gerald Pfeiffer's Bureau voiceprint (still on file, as federal law prohibits the deletion of biometric data associated with Rogue Voider proceedings, even posthumously). They are presented here in their probable chronological order, with minor edits for intelligibility. Gaps in the narrative are noted where they occur.*

*The Bureau of Biological Compliance was dissolved by legislative act in 2041. Director Maureen Trask's subsequent indictment and trial are a matter of separate public record.*

*These tapes are released as part of the Bureau Records Transparency Initiative. The Initiative's editorial board neither endorses nor disputes any claims made by Gerald Pfeiffer in these recordings. Certain statements may reflect the distorted perceptions of an individual under extreme psychological duress. Listeners are encouraged to consult the official Bureau post-dissolution FAQ, available at compliancearchive.gov, for context.*

*— Dr. Anika Feld, Chief Archivist, Bureau Records Transparency Initiative, 2043*

---

## TAPE 5

*(Believed to be May 14, 2035. The first surviving recording. Tape begins mid-sentence. Background hum consistent with a residential heating unit. Intermittent sound of what audio technicians describe as "fingernails on laminate.")*

— fourth time I've tried this because the first three I couldn't — I kept — look, the point is the following. The point is the following.

My name is Gerald Pfeiffer. I am — I *was* — a Certified Flush Auditor, Grade 11, Northeast Regional Division, and I have been compliant every single day of my adult life. I have the records. I have the stamps. I have the — the whole — I was *commended*, in 2031, I received the Director's Seal of Depositional Integrity, which is — for those who might someday hear this, and I realize I may be talking to no one, which is fine, which is consistent with the rest of my — anyway, the Director's Seal is awarded annually to one auditor per region whose personal Output Compliance Ratio exceeds 99.97 percent across all monitored categories for a continuous five-year period. Mine was 99.993. Director Trask signed it herself. I have the certificate. I had a frame for it. Custom. Forty-one dollars.

*(Pause. Sound of breathing. Seven seconds.)*

They spray-painted it. The frame. And the certificate, obviously, the certificate inside the frame. Someone — I don't know who, I didn't see, I was in the back bathroom, which I know how that sounds, I know exactly how that sounds, but I was in the back bathroom *with the door open and the sensor active* because I am not — I am not what they're saying. The sensor log will reflect — the sensor log *does* reflect — if anyone — the graffiti said FLUSH THE VOIDER. That's what they painted. On my certificate. On the glass over my certificate. In red.

I scraped it off. Most of it.

*(Pause.)*

I should back up. I should be systematic about this because if these recordings ever matter, if there is ever an inquiry, a review, even a — even a disciplinary subcommittee, which I would actually welcome at this point, I would *welcome* a disciplinary subcommittee because a subcommittee has procedures, it has evidentiary standards, it has — you can face your accuser in a disciplinary subcommittee. You sit across a table from them in a room with fluorescent lighting and they have to look at you.

Nobody is looking at me.

That's not — I don't mean that in a — I mean literally. Lena from next door, who I have waved to every morning for eleven years, she has placed a biohazard cordon across the property line. I didn't know you could buy biohazard tape at a hardware store. Maybe she got it online. It's yellow. It says CAUTION BIOLOGICAL HAZARD in black letters and she has strung it between my mailbox and her garden gnome, which is — it's about forty-five feet, which is a lot of tape, which means she ordered it in bulk, which means this wasn't *spontaneous*.

Okay. Systematic.

On May 9th, five days ago, Director Maureen Trask held a nationally broadcast compliance address — the monthly address, the one she does from the Bureau's Great Reclamation Hall, which is — you've seen it, everyone has seen it, it's the hall with the marble columns and the recessed deposit verification displays, very dignified, very — it communicates the seriousness — and during this address, Director Trask announced that the Bureau had identified a Rogue Voider operating within its own ranks.

An auditor. A Certified Flush Auditor.

She didn't name me during the broadcast. My name was released by the Bureau's Communications Office four hours later, in what they titled a "Compliance Threat Notification." Which went to every registered household in the Northeast Region. Sixty-two million households. My name. My Bureau ID. My address. My *photograph*. The photograph from my ID badge, the one where I'm squinting because the camera flash — they used *that* one.

*(Pause.)*

For those — and again, I may be talking to myself, which — for those unfamiliar, a "Rogue Voider" is — the formal statutory designation is "Unsanctioned Biological Depositor, Class A," which under the Integrated Defecation Security Act of 2024 is defined as any individual who knowingly produces, expels, or otherwise facilitates the generation of unmonitored fecal or urinary output in a location lacking certified deposit verification sensors with the intent to evade the biological compliance monitoring infrastructure of the Bureau. That's the letter of the statute. I know it by heart because I've enforced it. I have *enforced this statute*. Sixty-three successful audits leading to Rogue Voider prosecution referrals over my career. Sixty-three.

The penalty is — the maximum penalty — I need to be precise here. Under the 2024 Act as amended by the Supplemental Rectal Security Provisions of 2029, a Class A Unsanctioned Biological Depositor conviction carries a mandatory minimum of fifteen years in a Full Surveillance Containment Facility, which means — it means a cell with a transparent toilet. A transparent toilet that live-streams. To a monitoring audience. Twenty-four hours a day. For fifteen years.

That's the minimum.

The maximum — and the maximum is what Director Trask recommended in her address, she *specifically recommended* it, which is — it's unprecedented for the Director to recommend sentencing during the identification phase, that's — that shouldn't happen, that's a separation-of-process violation, I looked it up, it is — the maximum is Final Flush.

I shouldn't have to explain what Final Flush is. Everyone knows what Final Flush is. You've seen the public ceremonies. You've seen the — it's on the screens in the compliance plazas. I've seen fourteen of them and I never — I enforced the statute. I filed audits that led to — I believed in the necessity of — because the system works. The system only works if everyone is in the system. That's what Director Trask says. That's what she's *always* said. "The body is public. The output is communal. The unmonitored movement is a movement against us all." That's from her 2027 address, the one after the Chicago Disconnection Event, and when she said it I — I felt it. I felt the truth of it in my — I am not a dissident. I need to say that very clearly into this recording. I am not a dissident, I am not a Voider, I am not an enemy of the monitored community. I am a Certified Flush Auditor who has been compliant every single day of his adult life and I am being — 

*(Sound of glass breaking. Distant. Possibly external to the residence. Gerald's breathing accelerates.)*

That's them again. The — I don't know what to call them. Neighborhood compliance volunteers. That's the official — but they're not volunteers, they're a *mob*, they've been outside since the tenth, they have signs. I can hear them through the windows. They chant. The main chant is "Flush the Voider," pretty self-explanatory, and then there's a secondary chant that someone started on the second night, which is — it's more creative, I'll give them that — "Check his logs, check his bowl, drag the Voider from his hole," which doesn't — "hole" doesn't even rhyme with "bowl" if you — well, it's a slant rhyme, I suppose, if you're being generous, which I am not inclined to be because *they are outside my home calling for my execution*.

*(Silence. Twelve seconds.)*

I'm going to fight this. I need to say that. I'm going to fight this the right way, the way it should be fought, through Excretion Court, through the proper filings, because I have rights under the Integrated Defecation Security Act and those rights include the right to an Evidentiary Bowel Hearing before a jury of output-neutral peers, and I intend to exercise those rights. Because the system works. The system has to work because if the system doesn't work then — 

Then nothing that I've done mattered.

That's — I don't want to think about that.

I'm going to file the paperwork tomorrow. My FlushPass has been revoked, which means I can't use the monitored transit system, which means I'll have to walk to the regional courthouse, which is — it's eleven miles, but fine. Fine. I'll walk. I had a bowel movement at 6:47 this morning, fully logged, sensor-verified, normal consistency, and I can provide that record to anyone who — 

I'm going to fight this.

*(Tape ends.)*

---

## TAPE 6

*(Believed to be May 16, 2035. Considerable background noise: what audio analysts identify as "institutional echo" consistent with a large public building. A woman's voice is faintly audible in the background for the first forty seconds, repeating what may be the phrase "docket number." Gerald's voice is lower, more controlled than on Tape 5, and he appears to be whispering into the recorder.)*

I'm inside the courthouse of the Third Circuit Excretion Court of the Northeast Region, which took me — I walked, as anticipated, eleven miles, most of it along Route 9, and I was recognized twice. The first time, a man in a pickup truck slowed down and held up a hand-lettered sign that said ROGUE VOIDERS DESERVE THE BOWL. I don't know what "the bowl" means in this context. The second time, a woman at a gas station refused to let me use the restroom, which — under the FlushPass Revocation Protocol, I am legally required to *use only my home sensor unit* until trial, so I wouldn't have used her restroom anyway, but she didn't know that. She just saw my face and said no and locked the door. The face from the Compliance Threat Notification.

I held it for the entire walk. Eleven miles. For the record.

Court is — I want to describe this because I think it matters. The courtroom is on the fourth floor. It's a large room, wood-paneled, with the Bureau crest on the wall behind the judge's bench — the crest is the one with the two clasped hands holding a monitored deposit receptacle above the motto, "IN COMPLIANCE WE TRUST." There are fluorescent lights. The jury box has fourteen seats because under the Supplemental Rectal Security Provisions a Rogue Voider trial requires fourteen jurors rather than twelve, the additional two being what are called "Output Witnesses," whose role — and this is a little unusual — whose role is not to vote on the verdict but to be present in the courtroom restroom during juror bathroom breaks to verify that no juror has been emotionally compromised by testimony to the point of off-grid output event. I didn't write the law. I enforced it.

I have been assigned a defense attorney. His name is Clive Mendt. He is a Certified Bowel Barrister. He has a mustache that looks like it was grown to communicate seriousness and has instead communicated the opposite. When I met him in the hallway outside the courtroom, the first thing he said to me was, "I should be upfront — I've never handled a Class A." The second thing he said was, "But I did very well in Urinary Torts."

*(Pause.)*

The prosecution team is — there are four of them. Four attorneys, plus a Compliance Forensics Liaison, plus a Bureau Stool Analyst — the Stool Analyst, for those unaware, is a specialized technician who testifies to the chain-of-custody integrity of fecal sample evidence and provides the court with what's called a "Depositional Profile" of the accused. The Depositional Profile is a comprehensive biochemical and volumetric analysis of the defendant's output history, cross-referenced against sensor data from every registered toilet the defendant has used in the preceding five years. The prosecution has my Depositional Profile. They produced it during the preliminary motions hearing this morning and it was — it's a binder. A large binder. My entire biological life, in a binder, sitting on a table ten feet from me while a judge whose nameplate says HON. REGINALD THACKER, CERTIFIED ADJUDICATOR OF EXCRETORY MATTERS, reviewed it with what I can only describe as an expression of theatrical gravity.

The charge — the formal charge, as read aloud by the clerk — is that on or about March 22, 2035, I, Gerald R. Pfeiffer, FA-4409-GL, did knowingly produce an unmonitored bowel movement at an unregistered location, in violation of Sections 4, 7, and 12(b) of the Integrated Defecation Security Act, and that said unmonitored movement constituted "an act of biological terrorism against the monitored community."

I sat there and listened to the clerk read that and I thought: I was at work on March 22nd. I was in the field. I was conducting a routine audit. And my sensor logs from that day — all three registered movements — are clean. 7:12 a.m., home unit, verified. 12:40 p.m., Bureau regional office, Unit 7-C, verified. 5:55 p.m., home unit, verified. Three movements. Three verifications. Consistency scores within normal range. I have the printouts. I brought the printouts to court.

Clive Mendt looked at my printouts and said, "These are good. These are very solid logs." Then he said, "The problem is that they're alleging a *fourth* movement."

A fourth movement. On a three-movement day. The Bureau is claiming I produced an unmonitored fourth movement at an unregistered facility sometime between my 12:40 p.m. office deposit and my 5:55 p.m. home deposit. During my field audit hours. When I was — 

When I was at the facility. The facility I was auditing.

I want — I need to move on. There's a procedural matter I need to record. During the preliminary motions, Clive Mendt raised three objections, two of which were sustained and one of which was denied. The denied objection concerned
